record.paper_title: Unsolved Problems in Ordered and Orderable Groups
record.original_question: What can one say about quasi-finitely axiomatisable (QFA) ℓ-groups, abelian ℓ-groups and totally ordered groups. (A finitely generated model G of an algebraic theory T is said to be QFA if there is a sentence σ which holds in G such that every finitely generated model of T which satisfies σ is isomorphic to G).

evidence.quote: 1.57∗ . (G. Sabbagh) What can one say about quasi-finitely axiomatisable (QFA) ℓ-groups, abelian ℓ-groups and totally ordered groups. (A finitely generated model G of an algebraic theory T is said to be QFA if there is a sentence σ which holds in G such that every finitely generated model of T which satisfies σ is isomorphic to G).

artifact.self_contained_problem:
An algebraic structure $G$ that is a finitely generated model of an algebraic theory $T$ is called quasi-finitely axiomatisable (QFA) if there exists a first-order sentence $\sigma$ in the language of $T$ such that $G \models \sigma$ and every finitely generated model of $T$ satisfying $\sigma$ is isomorphic to $G$.

Recall that a lattice-ordered group (ℓ-group) is a group $(G,\cdot,e,{}^{-1})$ equipped with a lattice order $(\wedge,\vee)$ such that the group operation is order-preserving in both arguments (equivalently, $a(b\wedge c)d = abd \wedge acd$ and $a(b\vee c)d = abd \vee acd$ for all $a,b,c,d\in G$). An abelian ℓ-group is a commutative ℓ-group, and a totally ordered group is an ℓ-group whose lattice order is a total (linear) order.

Investigate and characterise the quasi-finitely axiomatisable structures within each of the following classes:

(a) ℓ-groups,
(b) abelian ℓ-groups,
(c) totally ordered groups.

Specifically, give a structural description (or necessary and sufficient conditions) of those finitely generated members of each class that are QFA in the corresponding first-order language, and exhibit nontrivial examples and obstructions.
artifact.status_search_result: While substantial progress has been made on QFA in related settings (e.g., Oger–Sabbagh's characterisation of QFA finitely generated nilpotent groups as prime models of their theories, and work on polycyclic-by-finite groups and finitely generated commutative rings), no source found in the search specifically resolves the question for ℓ-groups, abelian ℓ-groups, or totally ordered groups. The status appears to be unknown / open in the lattice-ordered setting.

status_evidence.title: Quasi-finitely axiomatizable nilpotent groups (Oger–Sabbagh)
status_evidence.snippet: A finitely generated nilpotent group is QFA iff it is a prime model of its complete theory.
status_evidence.claim: QFA is characterised in the nilpotent-group setting, but not for ℓ-groups.

status_evidence.title: Polycyclic-by-finite groups and first-order sentences
status_evidence.snippet: Studies QFA-type axiomatisability for polycyclic-by-finite groups.
status_evidence.claim: Related QFA results exist for other classes of groups, but not for lattice-ordered groups.

status_evidence.title: Unsolved Problems in Ordered and Orderable Groups
status_evidence.snippet: Sabbagh's question on QFA ℓ-groups, abelian ℓ-groups, and totally ordered groups is listed as an open problem.
status_evidence.claim: The question is recorded as an open problem in the literature on ordered groups.
